To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

IAT measures predict criterion measures with a mean effect size of r =.27, that this effect size is significantly larger than zero, that the IAT predicts criterion measures significantly better than self-report measures, that the IAN predicts criterion measures significantly beyond self-report, that the IIT predicts criterion measures beyond self-report, and that the IIT is more predictive of criterion measures when self-report measures are less predictive.

(1) IAT measures are moderately predictive of criterion measures and (2) IAT measures add predictive validity to explicit measures, especially in predicting socially sensitive criteria and when explicit measures are susceptible to impression management.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
IAT measures are valid predictors of behavior, judgment, and physiology, but that they do not predict as well as do parallel self-report measures.
IAT measures predict criterion measures significantly and reliably, with average effect sizes that are substantial and meaningful.
IAT and parallel self-report measures are both effective predictors of a broad variety of criterion measures.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
IAT measures are valid predictors, but that their validity is substantially limited by the validity of the self-report measures that are available for comparison.
IAT measures are valid and reliable predictors of behavior, but that their validity depends on the validity of parallel self-report measures.
the predictive validity of implicit measures is generally comparable to that of explicit measures.
The main takeaway from our work is that
IAT measures are valid predictors of behavior.
the IAT is a powerful tool for understanding the implicit associations that people hold and the effects that these implicit associations have on people’s behavior.
